text: A single engineer on call can usually fix a single-service outage alone — they look at the dashboards, find the bad deploy, and roll it back. That model breaks the moment an incident crosses team boundaries. If the person doing the hands-on debugging is also running the incident, answering Slack questions, and drafting status updates, the actual technical work slows to a crawl. That's why mature incident response, the kind Google's SRE practice popularized and most engineering orgs now run some version of, splits running the incident from fixing it into separate roles held by separate people.

The Incident Commander owns the incident as a process, not as a technical problem — deciding who works what, when to escalate, and when to accept a risky trade-off, but never personally touching the keyboard to apply the fix. The Communications Lead becomes the single voice for anything leaving the incident channel, so five different people aren't answering the same question with five slightly different answers. And the Scribe has one continuous job: capture what's happening, when, in a shared timeline, so nobody has to reconstruct the incident from memory later.

Here's what that timeline actually looks like in practice — a plain, timestamped log: alerts firing, the incident getting declared, each team joining and what they found, every hypothesis tested, the rollback, and recovery. That log isn't busywork. It becomes the primary input to the postmortem in Lesson 8, built from real timestamps instead of scattered chat scrollback pieced together days after the fact.

None of this means every page needs four people standing by. A quick, single-team SEV3 still gets handled solo, the same way it always has. The roles exist specifically for the moment an incident grows past one team, so there's already a known structure to step into instead of inventing coordination on the fly while the outage is still live — and on a long-running major incident, even the IC role can split further, with a Deputy IC taking over so the primary can rest.

That's the core role set: Incident Commander, Communications Lead, Scribe — three jobs, three people, once an incident stops being a one-team problem. Next lesson, you'll see how those roles actually coordinate five teams at once without each one debugging in isolation, using a single incident channel and a clear escalation path instead of ad hoc Slack DMs.
